sentences.text:
This petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. has been filed by the petitioners for quashing of the FIR dated 5.2.2019 registered at Crime No.52/2019 at Police Station Jhansi Road, Gwalior for offence punishable under Sections 420, 341, 506, 34 of IPC.
2.

The prosecution case as set forth in the FIR is that on 05.02.2019, the complainant, Shri Kamlesh Chaurasiya, lodged a written report alleging that he is engaged in business under the name and style of Yash Construction and Consultancy.

During the course of his business dealings, he came into acquaintance with the present petitioner, Shri Prafull Sharma, who developed close personal and family relations with the complainant, thereby gaining his trust and confidence.
The petitioner demanded a sum of Rs. 17,00,000/- from the complainant for his personal use.

Acting upon the said request and NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26031 2 MCRC-10363-2019 in good faith, the complainant allegedly paid an amount of Rs. 17,00,000/- in cash to the petitioner on 18.07.2016, for which a written agreement was executed stipulating that the said amount would be repaid by 30.07.2016.

The petitioner issued two cheques amounting in total to Rs. 17,00,000/-
towards repayment.
However, upon presentation, both cheques were dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds in the petitioner's account.

Subsequently, it is alleged that on 12.11.2017, the petitioner visited the residence of the complainant and requested the return of the previously issued Prafull Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 7 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107173628/
1 cheques, assuring that he would issue another cheque in their place.

sentences.text: Believing the petitioner's assurance, the complainant returned the old cheques, whereafter the petitioner allegedly brandished a pistol and fled from the spot.
A report regarding this incident was lodged on 13.11.2017.

Further,
the complaint records that on 05.02.2019, the complainant allegedly saw the petitioner riding an Activa scooter bearing registration no. MP07-SF-7779.

The petitioner stopped the complainant,
confronted him regarding the report filed against him, and that another individual named Sangam Tyagi, who was with the petitioner at that time, also threatened the complainant.
On the basis of these allegations, the instant FIR came to be registered against the present petitioners.

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner argued that the allegations levelled against the present petitioner are false, fabricated, and motivated, and that the registration of the FIR in question amounts to an abuse of the process of law.
The alleged transaction pertains to a purely civil dispute arising out of a financial arrangement between the parties.

The alleged NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:26031 3 MCRC-10363-2019 dishonour of cheques, if true, falls squarely within the purview of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, for which appropriate remedy lies before the competent court.
The attempt to give a criminal colour to a civil dispute is wholly impermissible in law.
It is further argued that the FIR was lodged after an unexplained and inordinate delay, which clearly indicates malafide intent on the part of the complainant to harass the petitioners.
The incident allegedly involving the pistol and subsequent confrontation is highly improbable and concocted, intended only to bolster a false narrative.
Learned counsel further argues that the petitioner is a law-abiding citizen and has been falsely implicated in the present matter with an ulterior motive to exert undue pressure and extract money.
It has further been argued that the present case is a clear example of misuse of the process of law by the complainant in connivance with certain police officials.
The entire case has been deliberately fabricated and planned with the sole intention of harassing the petitioners and grabbing their property.
The complainant, in collusion with one Vivek Singh Tomar, has been continuously lodging false and frivolous cases against the present petitioners.
Their motive is to illegally take possession of the property belonging to petitioner Prafull Sharma.
The daughter of petitioner no.2, namely Komal, was engaged to be married to petitioner Prafull Sharma on 15.02.2019.
However, due to registration of a series of false criminal cases at the instance of the complainant and Vivek Singh Tomar, the said marriage could not take place.
The complainant, in active collusion with Vivek Singh Tomar has got several false FIRs registered, including the present one.
Therefore, this FIR itself deserves to be quashed.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26031 4 MCRC-10363-2019 4.
It has further been argued that the complainant, in collusion with Vivek Singh Tomar, managed to get an FIR registered as Crime No. 458/2018, under Sections 420 and 406 of the IPC.
A perusal of that FIR shows that the alleged incident was more than two and a half years old, and the dispute raised was purely civil in nature.

In fact, in that transaction, it was petitioner no.2 who was cheated,
yet the FIR was registered under political pressure.
Even a bare reading of the said FIR shows that no offence was made out against the petitioners.
The registration of that case was done only to falsely implicate the petitioners and to create pressure upon them to part with their property.
It has further been argued that in order to create additional pressure, the complainant and Vivek Singh Tomar got another FIR registered as Crime No. 705/2018, under Sections 406 and 34 of the IPC.

sentences.text: The said case is again a gross abuse of process of law, as it arises out of a purely loan-based civil transaction which has been deliberately given the colour of a criminal offence.
The complainant's clear intention is to take over the mining business of petitioner Prafull Sharma, who was to become the son-in-law of petitioner no.2.
Learned counsel further argues that the present dispute is purely civil in nature.
The alleged transaction was a loan transaction, and mere failure to return borrowed money cannot constitute the offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC.
There is no allegation in the entire complaint that, from the inception, the petitioner had any dishonest intention to cheat the complainant.
Unless such intent is shown at the very beginning of the transaction, the offence of cheating is not made out.

Further, in the entire FIR, no specific role has been attributed to petitioner no.2 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26031 5 MCRC-10363-2019 regarding any act of cheating or criminal breach of trust.
This clearly shows that petitioner no.2 has been falsely implicated only to increase pressure upon petitioner no.1.
It is thus submitted that the dispute between the parties is essentially civil in nature, but has been maliciously given a criminal colour to exert undue pressure upon the petitioners.
5. Per contra, learned counsel for respondents opposed the petition and prays for its rejection.

It s argued that from the surrounding circumstances, the presence of mens rea is clearly established,
which is a necessary ingredient for constituting the offence under Section 420, 341, 506, 34 of IPC.

6. Heard counsel for the parties and perused the record.
7.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of International Advanced Research Centre For Powder Metallurgy and New Materials (ARCI) & Ors. v. Nimra Cerglass Technics Private Limited and Anr.
reported in (2016) 1 SCC 348 while interpreting the definition of cheating has laid down the law as under :-
"15.

sentences.text:
The essential ingredients to attract Section 420 I.P.C. are: (i) cheating; (ii)
dishonest inducement to deliver property or to make, alter or destroy any valuable security or anything which is sealed or signed or is capable of being converted into a valuable security and (iii) mens rea of the accused at the time of making the inducement.
The making of a false representation is one of the essential ingredients to constitute the offence of cheating under Section 420 I.P.C.

In order to bring a case for the offence of cheating, it is not merely sufficient to prove that a false representation had been made, but, it is further necessary to prove that the representation was false to the knowledge of the accused and was made in order to deceive the complainant.

16. Distinction between mere breach of contract and the cheating would depend upon the intention of the accused at the time of NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:26031 6 MCRC-10363-2019 alleged inducement.

If it is established that the intention of the accused was dishonest at the very time when he made a 1 Page 12 promise and entered into a transaction with the complainant to part with his property or money, then the liability is criminal and the accused is guilty of the offence of cheating.

On the other hand, if all that is established that a Prafull Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 7 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107173628/
3 representation made by the accused has subsequently not been kept, criminal liability cannot be foisted on the accused and the only right which the complainant acquires is the remedy for breach of contract in a civil court.

sentences.text: Mere breach of contract cannot give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown at the beginning of the transaction.

In S.W. Palanitkar & Ors. vs. State of Bihar & Anr. (2002) 1 SCC 241, this Court held as under:
"21 ......In order to constitute an offence of cheating, the intention to deceive should be in existence at the time when the inducement was made.

entities.text: S.W. Palanitkar & Ors. vs. State of Bihar & Anr. (2002) 1 SCC 241
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is necessary to show that a person had fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise, to say that he committed an act of cheating.
A mere failure to keep up promise subsequently cannot be presumed as an act leading to cheating."

The above view in Palanitkar's case was referred to and followed in Rashmi Jain vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr. (2014) 13 SCC 553"
8.

sentences.text:
A careful perusal of the FIR and the material collected during investigation reveals that the allegations do not disclose the existence of any fraudulent or dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, which is a sine qua non for constituting an offence under Section 420 IPC.
9.

Upon consideration of the submissions made by learned counsel for the petitioners and on perusal of the record, it appears that the present case is false, frivolous, and malicious, and has been registered only with a view to harass and pressurize the petitioners.
The entire dispute between the parties arises out of a purely civil transaction relating to a private financial arrangement.

The complainant, with the help of one Vivek Singh Tomar, has deliberately given this civil dispute a criminal colour in order to create undue NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26031 7 MCRC-10363-2019 pressure upon the petitioners and to grab their property and business.

It is evident from the record that there has been unexplained delay in lodging the FIR, and that no dishonest intention has been attributed to the petitioners at the inception of the alleged transaction.
In the absence of such intention, the essential ingredients of cheating under Section 420 IPC are not made out.

It is further clear that the complainant has been habitually filing false and frivolous complaints against the petitioners in collusion with others, with the ulterior motive of causing harassment and obstructing the marriage and business interests of petitioner Prafull Sharma.

Upon careful consideration of the facts as alleged, it appears that the petitioner, namely Prafull Sharma,
along with one other person, stopped the complainant on a public pathway near Science College and engaged in a verbal exchange regarding a prior monetary transaction.

Although it is alleged that the accused obstructed the complainant momentarily and issued certain threats, there is no material to suggest that the complainant was wrongfully restrained in a manner so as to prevent him from proceeding in any direction in which he had a right to move.

Mere stopping of the complainant for a brief conversation or altercation, without any continued or intentional prevention of movement,
does not satisfy the essential ingredients of Section 341 of the IPC, which requires proof of deliberate and unlawful obstruction of a person's free passage.

Therefore, from the facts it is clear that the Prafull Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 7 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107173628/
4 offence of wrongful restraint under Section 341 IPC is not made out against the petitioner.

At best,
the allegations may disclose a verbal dispute or exchange of words, but they fall short of constituting the offence punishable under Section 341 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26031 8 MCRC-10363-2019 IPC.

It is thus found that the FIR is based on false and baseless allegations and that the dispute, if any, is purely civil in nature but has been maliciously given a criminal colour to harass the petitioners.
The necessary ingredients of the offences under Sections 420, 341, 506, 34 of IPC are not made out.
The allegations, at best, indicate a civil dispute over title, which has been given a criminal colour.
10. On perusal of the FIR and the material collected during investigation, it is evident that the dispute thus falls squarely within the domain of a civil liability.

11. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Satish Mehra v. State (N.C.T. of Delhi) and Another , AIR 2013 SC 506 , has held that the inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. are wide and plenary in nature and may be exercised at any stage of criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of the process of law or to secure the ends of justice.

entities.text: Satish Mehra v. State (N.C.T. of Delhi) and Another , AIR 2013 SC 506
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It has been observed that where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint do not prima facie disclose the commission of a cognizable offence, the accused should not be compelled to undergo the rigours of a protracted criminal trial.
12. In the present case, even if the entire allegations in the FIR are taken at their face value, they merely disclose a civil dispute.
The initiation of criminal proceedings appears to be a device to settle personal scores.
Continuance of such prosecution would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court.

13. Accordingly, this Court is of the considered view that the FIR bearing Crime No.52/2019 registered at Police Station Jhansi Road, Gwalior, NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:26031 9 MCRC-10363-2019 for offences punishable under Sections 420, 341,
506, 34 of IPC against the petitioners and all consequential proceedings arising therefrom, deserve to be and are hereby quashed.
14. The petition is accordingly allowed.
No order as to costs.
